column1: What does WBS stand for on this sheet?
column2: Work Breakdown Structure — a code marking each task's place in the project hierarchy.

column1: Why assign a WBS code before writing the task itself?
column2: It fixes the task's position in the hierarchy, so subtasks stay attached to the right parent even after re-ordering.

column1: How should WBS codes be numbered for sub-tasks?
column2: Decimal notation such as 1.1, 1.2, 1.2.a — each added level shows one step deeper in the breakdown.

column1: What belongs in the Resource column?
column2: The person, role, or team responsible for the task — not necessarily whoever logged it.

column1: How is a task with two resources recorded on one row?
column2: Both names can be written in the Resource cell, or the task can be split into two rows sharing one WBS code with a letter suffix.

column1: How should the Start field be filled in?
column2: With the planned calendar date the task is meant to begin, written before work starts.

column1: What does Duration record?
column2: The planned length of the task in working days, not calendar days.

column1: Why measure Duration in working days rather than calendar days?
column2: Weekends are already shaded as rest days on the grid, so counting them again in Duration would double them up.

column1: What is the ETA column used for?
column2: The expected completion date, checked against actual progress at each review.

column1: What is the difference between ETA and the day actually shaded as finished?
column2: ETA is the forecast written in ink at the start; the last shaded day is the outcome — comparing the two shows how the estimate held up.

column1: How many weeks does one printed sheet cover?
column2: Four week-blocks, each with its own Monday-to-Sunday day grid.

column1: What is the Week No. field in the header for?
column2: The ISO week the first block starts on, so completed sheets can be filed and found by week number.

column1: What goes in the Date range field?
column2: The calendar span the four week-blocks cover, written once the sheet's start week is fixed.

column1: How is daily progress marked on the grid?
column2: Shade the cell for each day actually worked; Saturdays and Sundays are pre-shaded as default rest days.

column1: What should be done if a task runs past its planned duration?
column2: Extend the shading into the following days rather than erasing the plan — the drift is itself useful information.

column1: How can a milestone be distinguished from an ordinary task on the sheet?
column2: Give it a Duration of zero or one day and mark its single day cell with a distinct symbol, such as a diamond, instead of a plain shade.

column1: How can task dependencies be shown on a paper sheet with no arrows?
column2: By ordering dependent tasks on consecutive rows under the same parent WBS code, so the sequence reads top to bottom.

column1: How is a delay in one task carried over to a dependent task by hand?
column2: The dependent task's Start and ETA are crossed out and rewritten once the earlier task's actual finish day is known.

column1: What symbol convention keeps status readable at a glance?
column2: A consistent mark per state — for example a filled square for done, a diagonal line for in progress, and an empty cell for not started.

column1: Why use a pencil for the day grid and pen for the six label columns?
column2: Plans logged at the start (WBS, Task, Resource, Start, Duration, ETA) are meant to stay fixed, while day-by-day shading needs to be revisable as work actually happens.

column1: How can colour be used without changing the sheet's design?
column2: A highlighter can shade completed days, leaving the printed light-gray weekend fill as the only built-in colour cue.

column1: What is the weekly review step in this workflow?
column2: At the start of each week, shade the days completed and update any ETA that has slipped.

column1: What should happen at the end of the four-week period, before starting a new sheet?
column2: Every row is checked off as done, carried forward, or dropped, so nothing is lost between sheets.

column1: How can this sheet be linked to an index-card or notebook system?
column2: Write the task's WBS code on any card or page that documents that task, so both records can be cross-referenced.

column1: How does this sheet fit alongside a kanban-style task board?
column2: The Gantt sheet holds the time-based plan, while the kanban board tracks which phase each task is currently in — the WBS code is the link between the two.

column1: What should be filled in before any tasks are logged?
column2: The Project, Company, Project Manager, Week No., Date range, and Prepared by fields in the header.

column1: Why keep task details in fixed columns instead of inside the day grid?
column2: So who, when, and how long stay legible at a glance, separate from the day-by-day progress marks.

column1: What is the footer legend for?
column2: It reminds anyone reading a filled-in sheet what each column abbreviation means, without the original instructions.

column1: What should be done once a project runs past four weeks?
column2: Start a new sheet for the next four weeks and carry forward any open tasks under their original WBS codes.

column1: How should a large project be split across several sheets?
column2: By top-level WBS branch — each sheet covers one branch of the hierarchy rather than mixing unrelated branches on one page.

column1: Why choose the paper size (A4 or US Letter) before printing?
column2: To match the paper stock already in use and keep sheets a consistent size for filing.

column1: How should completed sheets be archived for later reference?
column2: Filed in Week No. order, so a project's full run of sheets reads in sequence when pulled later.

column1: How can a finished sheet be turned into a digital record?
column2: By photographing or scanning it and filing the image alongside its Week No., or by re-typing the row data into a spreadsheet for longer-term tracking.
